hero.label: Product Strategy & Execution
hero.body: I lead the product conversation from ambiguity to clarity — modeling the domain, clarifying the opportunity, and structuring the path from insight to working product.

heading: Most teams build
what's requested.

items.label: The Requirement Problem
items.body: Clients know their domain. They do not know what product will serve that domain best. The requirement is always a hypothesis — often a good one, rarely the final answer.

items.label: The Translation Problem
items.body: Between the client's intent and the development team lies a gap. Meetings, tickets, misunderstandings, rework. Most of the waste in software projects lives in this gap.

items.label: The Timing Problem
items.body: By the time most teams discover the product direction was wrong, months have passed. The prototype comes after the contract, not before it.

problem.pullQuoteBody: The intake session is not requirement gathering. It is domain research. By the time it concludes, the product direction is clear and grounded in reality.
problem.footnote: Grounded in Evans' Domain-Driven Design, Christensen's Jobs-to-Be-Done, and the British Design Council's Double Diamond framework.

stages.title: Intelligent Outreach
stages.body: Before you reach me, the system is already working. Market context, positioning signals, and product opportunities are being sensed and framed.

stages.title: Structured Intake
stages.body: You book. You provide context. The system begins domain research and prepares a briefing before the first session.

stages.title: Deep Session
stages.body: A small number of high-value conversations. I clarify, challenge, and expand the product model until the path is obvious.

stages.title: Parallel Build
stages.body: While the strategy is being refined, the prototype begins to take shape. The domain model is made concrete quickly.

stages.title: Convergence
stages.body: Requirements finalize. The demo is ready. Product direction is clear. The next steps are obvious because the model was grounded from the start.

cards.title: Product Strategy
cards.body: The system knows the domain, patterns, and constraints. It helps frame the product direction, sharpen the opportunity, and translate ambiguity into a strategy that can be tested quickly.
cards.footer: This is how the work starts.

cards.title: Delivery
cards.body: Once the product direction is clear, the same capability is applied to the client's domain and context. The result is not just a working build — it is a product introduced with clarity and intent.
cards.footer: Your product, positioned from day one.

trio.label: The Lead
heading: One role.
One clear product direction.
trio.closingQuote: I model the problem, shape the strategy, and turn ambiguity into a product path.

members.title: System Architect
members.plain: I figure out what actually needs to be built — and why.
members.body:
I think in systems before I think in code. My role is conceptual integrity — making sure the product reflects reality accurately, not just what was requested.

I am the primary knowledge cruncher in every intake session. By the end, the answer is clear: this is the product direction, and this is why.

page.heroSubtitle: I turn ambiguity into clarity. Strategy, structure, and product direction before execution.

philosophy.label: Philosophy
heading: Conceptual integrity
above all else.
philosophy.quote: The requirement is always a hypothesis — often a good one, rarely the final answer.
philosophy.quoteBody: I don't take requirements at face value. Every intake session is domain research — a structured excavation of what actually needs to exist.

items.title: Domain First
items.body: Before any architecture decision, understand the domain deeply. Software that reflects the domain accurately is software that works.

items.title: Conceptual Integrity
items.body: A system designed with clear intent will be coherent. Coherent systems are maintainable, explainable, and trusted.

items.title: Prescribe, Don't Transcribe
items.body: The client knows their domain. They do not know the solution space. My role is to prescribe what should be built — and articulate why.

items.title: Knowledge Crunching
items.body: Every conversation is an opportunity to sharpen the model. The product model is a living understanding that improves with each interaction.

stages.label: Before the Session
stages.body: The system prepares a domain briefing. I review it, identify gaps, and formulate the questions that will drive the conversation.

stages.label: During the Session
stages.body: I am the primary listener and questioner. Every answer is processed through the lens of domain modeling — what entities exist, what relationships matter, what the real constraints are.

stages.label: After the Session
stages.body: The product model is refined. I emerge with a clear direction and a grounded plan for execution, not just a stack of notes.

closing.quote: This is what you need, and this is why.
closing.attribution: — The Lead, at the end of every intake session

frameworks.label: The Foundation
heading: Every claim we make
is grounded.
frameworks.subheading: We did not invent these ideas. We are the first team operating all of them simultaneously, at agentic speed.

tiles.label: Domain-Driven Design · Evans, 2003
tiles.body: Developers who become domain experts are the most effective builders. The intake session is knowledge crunching — and it ends when the Lead knows the domain.
tiles.source: Eric Evans' official DDD resource hub — the primary home for the methodology.

tiles.label: Jobs-to-Be-Done · Christensen, Harvard
tiles.claim: The real need behind the stated requirement
tiles.body: Clients are experts in their own experience. They are not experts in the solution space. The Lead excavates the job beneath the requirement — and builds for that.
tiles.source: Original peer-reviewed article published by Harvard Business Review, September 2016.

tiles.label: Double Diamond · British Design Council, 2005
tiles.claim: Problem definition is half the work
tiles.body: Teams that define the right problem before building produce better outcomes. The Lead's intake is the first diamond — run before most teams start theirs.
tiles.source: The Design Council's own page for their own framework. Nothing more authoritative exists.

tiles.label: Lean Startup · Ries, 2011
tiles.claim: The prototype is a hypothesis, not a promise
tiles.body: The parallel build during intake is not a bet on correct requirements. It is the Build-Measure-Learn loop run at the intake stage — making the alignment conversation concrete.
tiles.source: Eric Ries' official Lean Startup methodology page — the principles, in full, for free.

tiles.label: The Trusted Advisor · Maister, Green & Galford
tiles.claim: Trust is earned through demonstrated competence
tiles.body: Trustworthiness = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) ÷ Self-Orientation. The intake system is designed to address all four variables directly.
tiles.source: The Trust Equation — explained in full on the authors' own firm's website.

tiles.label: Agentic Coding Trends · Anthropic, 2026
tiles.claim: Small teams with agentic tools outperform large teams
tiles.body: One engineer can now maintain systems that previously required teams. A single lead-led operating model is designed around this reality.
tiles.source: Anthropic's official 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report. Note: download requires an email.

portfolio.subheading: Filed by how the work was shaped.

items.label: Why
items.body: Cafés, bars, and restaurants need a real digital presence — menu, ambiance, story — but rarely have the budget or timeline for a bespoke build. The requirement is nearly the same shape every time: show the place, make it feel like the place, get people through the door.

items.label: How
items.body: Built once as a repeatable system rather than reinvented per client. Same underlying framework and build pipeline; only the content shifts — menu, photography, voice, and layout emphasis per venue. New venues ship against that same system, not a new architecture.

items.label: Where It's Heading
items.body: The pattern that emerged from repetition — one system serving many independent venues — is the same shape the Multi-Tenant work formalizes. Hospitality is where the idea proved itself before it became a platform.

items.label: Why
items.body: Not every request fits a template. An enterprise services company, a spiritual information platform, and this landing page itself — each has its own domain, audience, and constraints that don't reduce to 'venue website.'

items.label: How
items.body: Each build starts from the client's actual domain, not a starting template. Information architecture, content, and design are worked out case by case, from scratch.

items.label: Where It's Heading

items.label: Why
items.body: A single-venue website solves presence, not operations. Parlor owners didn't need another page — they needed a way to actually run bookings, day to day.

items.label: How
items.body: Built as one platform serving many parlor owners, not one site per owner. Customers book through a guided step-by-step flow; each owner runs their day from a live dashboard of today's, upcoming, and past appointments — same system, many tenants.

items.label: Where It's Heading
items.body: This is the direction the Hospitality work points toward — fewer bespoke venue sites, more shared platforms that give owners real operational leverage instead of just a page.

items.label: Why
items.body: Multi-outlet retailers in Biratnagar often rely on phone calls, spreadsheets, and manual reconciliation to understand sales, stock, and store performance. As more outlets are added, inventory transfers, procurement, staff permissions, discounts, and IRD compliance become difficult to coordinate, leaving owners with delayed decisions instead of real-time visibility.

items.label: How
items.body: Built as a single retail management platform serving every outlet from one system. Cashiers use a streamlined POS terminal, managers oversee procurement and stock transfers, warehouse teams handle inventory movement, accountants work from an append-only financial ledger, and owners monitor every store through a live dashboard. Role-based access, approval workflows, inventory validation, discount controls, audit trails, and IRD-ready operations keep every part of the business connected.

items.label: Where It's Heading
items.body: This represents the future of retail software—moving beyond standalone POS systems into complete operational platforms where sales, inventory, finance, compliance, and decision-making operate from a single source of truth across every outlet.

projects.title: Caliber Retail Management
projects.description: A multi-outlet retail management platform that gives business owners complete visibility across every store. It combines POS, inventory, procurement, stock transfers, role-based access, approval workflows, discount management, audit trails, financial reporting, and IRD-ready operations into one unified system.
